messages.subject: Re: Model not identified when all Items covaried to each other (But it works in AMOS)
messages.subject_clean: Model not identified when all Items covaried to each other (But it works in AMOS)
messages.body_plain:
Common factors are defined by the covariance among indicators that is not otherwise accounted for. Allowing covariance among residuals reduces the unexplained common variance that is available for defining common factors. Moreover, allowing covariances among residuals consume degrees of freedom, and edge the model toward not being statistically identified, which can mean that the model cannot be estimated at all. The rules are the same for the Amos implementation of factor analysis as for the lavaan implementation--I don't know why Amos would not produce the same sort of error message that you are getting from lavaan.

In your syntax, NOT EVERY item's residual is free to covary with that of every other item loading on the same factor. So I suppose it is possible that small differences in things like starting values could have produced a different result with Amos. Nevertheless, there is no reason to expect a good results from a model like this.

messages.body_plain:
> This didn't make sense to me because r^2 is the relative amount of variance of the dependent variable explained by the IVs, but the kittens are the just items that make up a construct.

Factor loadings are regression slopes.  Indicators are DVs, and the latent construct is (hypothesized to be) their common cause ("common factor") that accounts for their covariance.  The R^2 for an indicator is the proportion of its variance that is explained by the common factor, and the remaining portion is due to item-specific uniqueness (including measurement error).

> In any case, I saw all of these values, and then arrived at the r^2 value for my key DV,

The R^2 for your DV of interest (the common factor being predicted by other IVs) is the only value you need to pay attention to.  It has the same interpretation is R^2 always does, so you can probably follow whatever advice you were already following for calculating ΔR^2.

> when I treat my data as ordinal, am getting zero values for intercepts. When I use continuous data am getting all intercepts. What might be the cause for zero intercepts?

Fitting a covariance-structure analysis model to ordinal data is only possible when we assume a normally distributed latent item response underlying each observed ordered (or binary) response. We can either fix the thresholds and estimate the intercepts, or we can fix the intercepts to zero and estimate the thresholds (which is what lavaan does).  See more details here:

http://www.statmodel.com/download/webnotes/CatMGLong.pdf

This isn't specific to lavaan, so if you have further questions that are about SEM in general, you can post them on the much larger forum called SEMNET:

messages.subject_clean: Discrepancy b2 bootstrap p-value and CIs?
messages.body_plain:
If you're using bootstrapping for inference, the p-value and CIs can disagree. The reason for this is that even when using bootstrapping to generate SEs the Wald statistic and associated p-value assume that the sampling distribution of your parameter is symmetric. However, with a bootstrap sampling distribution there's no guarantee this is the case, and the p value when using a bootstrapped SE isn't terribly informative. On the other hand, with a bootstrap CI, you're just taking the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles (for a 95% CI) from the bootstrap distribution (with some adjustments if you're using BC or BCA confidence intervals) with no assumption about the shape of a distribution. In this case, the CI should give you a more accurate picture of the sampling distribution than the p-value. I tell my students that if they are using bootstrapping to rely on CIs for inference as the p-value can be misleading.

Alex

On 10/15/2016 09:06 PM, kmarkus via lavaan wrote:
> When a model contains both an equality constraint  between parameters

> parameterEstimates() numbers the parameters non-sequentially (at least

> the equality constraints listed in the parameter table between the model
> parameters and defined parameters.

That is correct. The parameterEstimates() function simply provides a
convenient subset of the (larger) parTable() function. Because the focus
is on the parameter estimates themselves, we omit (by default) the rows
corresponding to equality constraints (or inequality constraints). But
we do include the defined parameters, because we are often interested in
their values (and SEs). And indeed, the 'id' column will have some
missing gaps in this case. That is the intended behavior.

> It appears that this does not affect
> equality constraints between parameters with the same name because they
> are listed last.

I am not sure what mean by this. Could you clarify?

> HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + a*x2 + b*x3
>               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
>               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9

>
> parameterEstimates(fit)[24:25,]

parameterEstimates(fit, remove.eq = FALSE)

but as you will see, the added information is not very useful.

lavaanify(HS.model, auto = TRUE)

Yves,
Sorry my post was unclear.

I am not sure what the intended use cases were for parameterEstimates() but I rely on it to extract defined parameter estimates and their SEs.  (In this case, I was computing a CI from the SEs of composite reliability, for example.)  For that purpose, it is helpful to have the elements numbered sequentially because it makes it easier to identify the correct index to extract the parameter.  The output is not wrong, it is just that sequential numbering might make it more user friendly.  That was the intention behind my post.

>> It appears that this does not affect
>> equality constraints between parameters with the same name because they
>> are listed last.
>
>I am not sure what mean by this. Could you clarify?

The point is of not great importance but let me clarify with an example.  If we run my original example (with an equality constraint between parameters with different names) we get the following in the parameter table:

> lavaanify(HS.model)[21:23,]
   id   lhs op   rhs user group free ustart exo label plabel
21 21 speed ~~ speed    0     1    0      0   0        .p21.
22 22     a ==     b    1     0    0     NA   0
23 23  nada :=     0    1     0    0     NA   0  nada
>

The equality constraint is listed on line 22 and the defined parameter afterwards on line 23.  This leads to the gap when the constraint is removed.  In contrast, consider the result when an equality constraint is imposed using the same name.

HS.model2 <- ' visual  =~ x1 + a*x2 + a*x3

              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9

              nada := 0 '

fit2 <- cfa(HS.model2, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)

parameterEstimates(fit2)[24:25,]
dim(parameterEstimates(fit2))
lavaanify(HS.model2)[21:23,]

Here is the result of the last line:

> lavaanify(HS.model2)[21:23,]
   id   lhs op   rhs user group free ustart exo label plabel
21 21 speed ~~ speed    0     1    0      0   0        .p21.
22 22  nada :=     0    1     0    0     NA   0  nada
23 23  .p2. ==  .p3.    2     0    0     NA   0
>

Here the constraint appears on line 23 below the defined parameter on line 22.  So, in this case, there will be no gap when the constraint is removed.  There are no surprises there.  I was just noting why the gaps only appear when different names are used.

Thanks for pointing out the auto=TRUE parameter for lavaanify().  I think that I had read the explanation in the help file before, but never understood what it did.  As in the above example, I got what I needed without it but it would have made the example clearer to have used this parameter.  So, it is good to finally understand what it does.

Dear all,
I was wondering what would be arguments against (always) constraining residual variances of observed variables to 1-factorloading^2 in cases where the variables are standardized. It seems it would save multiple df's without losing any information. I haven't seen it done in cases other than perhaps 'emergencies' to achieve identification (e.g. with one or two observed variables), but am wondering whether there are more principled reasons against doing so - Why spend a parameter on something that is known? I'm sure there are good reasons for it (overfitting, indirect 'data peeking'?) but I haven't found them yet. The below syntax reproduces simulated data and a freely estimated and a constrained version of a simple CFA. Unsurprisingly they yield virtually identical chi-squares, but the constrained model saves 5 df's.

modelsim<-'
lv1=~.8*x1+.7*x2+.6*x3+.4*x4+.3*x5
'

simdat<-simulateData(modelsim,sample.nobs = 500)
simdat<-scale(simdat)

fit_free<-'

lv1=~lambdx1*x1+NA*x1+lambdx2*x2+lambdx3*x3+lambdx4*x4+lambdx5*x5
lv1~~1*lv1
x1~~resvarx1*x1
x2~~resvarx2*x2
x3~~resvarx3*x3
x4~~resvarx4*x4
x5~~resvarx5*x5
'

fit_free_fit<-cfa(fit_free,data=simdat)
summary(fit_free_fit, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE, rsquare=TRUE)

fit_constraints<-'

lv1=~lambdx1*x1+NA*x1+lambdx2*x2+lambdx3*x3+lambdx4*x4+lambdx5*x5
x1~~resvarx1*x1
x2~~resvarx2*x2
x3~~resvarx3*x3
x4~~resvarx4*x4
x5~~resvarx5*x5
lv1~~1*lv1
resvarx1==1-lambdx1^2
resvarx2==1-lambdx2^2
resvarx3==1-lambdx3^2
resvarx4==1-lambdx4^2
resvarx5==1-lambdx5^2
'

fit_constraints_fit<-cfa(fit_constraints,data=simdat)
summary(fit_constraints_fit, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE, rsquare=TRUE)

> I was wondering what would be arguments against (always) constraining residual variances of observed variables to 1-factorloading^2 in cases where the variables are standardized. It seems it would save multiple df's without losing any information. I am wondering whether there are more principled reasons against doing so - Why spend a parameter on something that is known?

Here's the answer I would have posted on SEMNET if I saw it there :-)  You are hinting at the reasons why more recent SEM textbooks recommend always to analyze a covariance matrix, not a correlation matrix, and why lavaan will print a warning if it looks like you are analyzing a correlation matrix.  You are correct, when we use sample values to "standardize" (actually "studentize", if we use sample estimates of unknown parameters, in which case they are not standardized relative to anything outside our sample), the total variance must be 1 by definition.  You can think of it as using up a degree of freedom for each variable we studentize, because we are using a parameter estimate to do so.  Estimating (residual) variances that should be fixed when analyzing correlations leads to biased SEs, unless you either use special formulas to calculate SEs (which lavaan does using the standardizedSolution() function) or you appropriately constrain variances to 1, or residual variances to 1 - (explained variance), in your model syntax to begin with.  Here is an article that discusses these issues:

http://www.statpower.net/Content/319SEM/Reading/Cudeck89.pdf

Terrence D. Jorgensen

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Question about int.ov.free
messages.subject_clean: Question about int.ov.free
messages.body_plain:
> Why does int.ov.free need to be set to TRUE when doing multi-group analyses?

It doesn't need to be. You can specify the intercepts in your syntax instead.  But if you don't, and you leave int.ov.free - FALSE, then you are saying all intercepts are zero (in single- or multiple-group models).  That is only reasonable if you have mean-centered data, in which case you should probably omit set meanstructure = FALSE anyway (although that is not an option when using FIML or a robust correction).

> I get the same results when set to FALSE as I do when set to TRUE before doing a multi-group analysis, but I get very different results when conducting multi-group analyses such that if it's set to FALSE it's a very poorly fitting model.

That depends on the characteristics of your data, and what you mean by "same".  I think the default is meanstructure = FALSE for single-group models and meanstructure = TRUE for multiple-group models, at least when using the cfa() or sem() functions.  You can try out for yourself what happens when just using the lavaan() function with whatever arguments you are using.

> lavInspect(fit, "options")$meanstructure

The logic is that in a single-group, single-occasion model, the mean structure is probably saturated because in most situations there is no motivation to constrain means/intercepts, so the results are the same whether you include mean structure or not.  In longitudinal and multigroup models, it is interesting to compare means/intercepts across groups/occasions, so most of the time people will want to model the mean and covariance structure.

> Furthermore, I'm trying to wrap my head around another thought I had. If int.ov.free and int.lv.free constrain the intercepts to be 0, then shouldn't doing group.equal="intercepts" result in the same model fit?

Yes, with a "but".  The group.equal argument only applies to estimated parameters.  If they are fixed to specific values, they are not being estimated, so they will only be "constrained to equality" if they happen to be fixed to the same value (here, 0, so yes they would be equal).  But if you did estimate the intercepts and constrain them to equality, they would probably have nonzero estimated values that are equal across groups, which should fit the data better than constraining the intercepts to zero (unless your data are group-mean-centered).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
Would this give you what you need?

require(lavaan)

## The famous Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)

getRMR <- function(fit, ...){
  # Bollen (1989) page 257
  obs.cov <- lavInspect(fit, 'sampstat')$cov
  obs.cov <- obs.cov[lower.tri(obs.cov, diag=TRUE)]
  imp.cov <- lavInspect(fit, 'cov.ov')
  imp.cov <- imp.cov[lower.tri(imp.cov, diag=TRUE)]
  rmr <- mean((obs.cov - imp.cov)^2)^.5
  return(rmr)
}

getRMR(fit)

messages.subject: Re: semTools update
messages.subject_clean: semTools update
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Version 0.4-14 of semTools assimilates lavaan's most recent internal changes, so it requires at least lavaan version 0.5-22 (and therefore R >= 3.1).  Two new functions, provided by Terrence D. Jorgensen, are available: chisqSmallN() and twostage(), along with lavaan wrappers lavaan.2stage(), cfa.2stage(), sem.2stage(), and growth.2stage().  The first calculates a small-sample correction to the chi-squared test of model fit, as described in:

> Nevitt, J., & Hancock, G. R. (2004). Evaluating small sample approaches for model test statistics in structural equation modeling. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 39(3), 439-478. doi:10.1207/S15327906MBR3903_3

The latter functions implement 2-stage ML estimation to handle missing continuous data. You can read the details in:

> Savalei, V., & Bentler, P. M. (2009). A two-stage approach to missing data: Theory and application to auxiliary variables. Structural Equation Modeling, 16(3), 477-497. doi:10.1080/10705510903008238
>
> Savalei, V., & Falk, C. F. (2014). Robust two-stage approach outperforms robust full information maximum likelihood with incomplete nonnormal data. Structural Equation Modeling, 21(2), 280-302. doi:10.1080/10705511.2014.882692

A known issue with twostage() is that the Satorra-Bentler scaled test statistic of model fit appears too large.  Although the formulas appear correct in the source code, there may be an undiscovered bug.  For now, only use the residual-based test statistic of model fit, which assumes normally distributed data.  Future versions of semTools might also make alternative fit indices available, but for now the user must calculate them manually.  The baseline model is available in the fitted model object, so incremental fit indices such as CFI and TLI can be computed.

A bug was fixed in the permuteMeasEq() function, but there is still a known issue that will be fixed in the next update to semTools.  Windows users who try to use the parallel-computing options in permuteMeasEq() will receive an error because the objects in the global environment are not available on the SOCK clusters.  Mac and Linux users will not receive an error if they use Fork clusters or the "multicore" option because the clusters will have access to the global environment.

https://github.com/simsem/semTools/wiki

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
On 10/26/2016 03:13 PM, Torres wrote:
> Thank you Yves. I followed your instruction and I have rmr =.105 which
> is far greater than srmr= .045. I did not know how to explain such big
> difference.

But rmr is not srmr. rmr is the square root of the mean of the squared
raw residuals, while srmr is the square root of the mean of the
*standardized* residuals.

For example,

library(lavaan)
example(cfa)

# observed S
S <- lavInspect(fit, "observed")$cov
# implied Sigma
Sigma <- lavInspect(fit, "implied")$cov

R <- lav_matrix_vech(S - Sigma)
# RMR
sqrt(mean(R^2))
# 0.08218433

# SRMR (EQS style)
sqrt.d <- 1/sqrt(diag(S))
D <- diag(sqrt.d, ncol=length(sqrt.d))
ZR <- lav_matrix_vech( D %*% (S - Sigma) %*% D )
sqrt(mean(ZR^2))
# 0.06520506

Most people would be interested in the standardized version.

> Normally I get the information of some indices such as RMSEA, SRMR in
> the column of robust when I make use of estimator of MLM (robust form).
> But I could not find information of RMR at both ML as well as Robust
> column on the summary output. In my case, the score of rmr I got from
> fitMeasures(fit, "rmr") is the one that belongs to the Robust column,
> isn't it?

It does not matter: RMR or SRMR are the same for both plain ML or robust
ML. They are just based on the residuals.

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: Minor issue with parameterEstimates() function
messages.body_plain:
On 10/16/2016 10:27 PM, kmarkus via lavaan wrote:
> I am not sure what the intended use cases were for parameterEstimates()
> but I rely on it to extract defined parameter estimates and their SEs.
> (In this case, I was computing a CI from the SEs of composite
> reliability, for example.)  For that purpose, it is helpful to have the
> elements numbered sequentially because it makes it easier to identify
> the correct index to extract the parameter

I would never trust the 'id' column (perhaps I should remove it
altogether from the output), as it always reflects the original id
number from the 'full' parTable, but some rows may have been removed in
the output of parameterEstimates().

However, 'defined parameters' always have a name (the lhs of the :=
operator), and I would recommend to look up the name in the lhs column
to find the proper row index.

For example:

toyModel <- '
  f =~ x1 + x2 + a*x3 + b*x4
  ab := a*b
'
fit <- sem(toyModel, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)

PE <- parameterEstimates(fit)
# select 'ab' row:
PE[PE$lhs == "ab",]

Alternatively, if you only have a single ":=" in the table, you can use
PE[PE$op == ":=",]

Yves.

I no longer have access to Amos.  However, the term 'standardized residuals' can mean different things in different contexts.  Perhaps you are seeking what lavaan calls correlation residuals.  These are the raw residuals standardized to a correlation metric.  The standardized residuals are z scores.

>From the lavaan class help file:
>>>

If type="cor", the observed and model implied covariance matrix is first transformed to a correlation matrix (using cov2cor), before the residuals are computed. If
...

If type="standardized", the residuals are divided by the square root of the difference between an asymptotic variance estimate of the corresponding sample statistic and an asymptotic variance estimate of the corresponding model-implied statistic. In the latter case, the residuals have a metric similar to z-values.
>>>

------------------------

messages.body_plain:
The sample size issue is more complex than the number of items (namely, it depends how reliable the items are), but keep in mind that in a multiple group model you have parameters in each group, so you would need 15 people per item in each group, not overall.  Of course, constraints would mean you utilize information across groups, again, that rule of thumb is overly simplistic.  But this question is better suited for SEMNET because it has nothing to do with lavaan.

www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>

When you post on SEMNET, it might help to use clearer terminology, because I cannot tell from your description in which situation the groups vary and in which situation they do not appear to vary.  Measurement invariance means that the measurement parameters do not vary across groups (i.e., they are equal).  A synonym for measurement invariance is measurement equivalence, which I think is much easier for people to understand, so I encourage its use.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

behavior =~ Behavior
Behavior~~0*Behavior

sets the residual variance of the observed variable to 0, while the second form

behavior =~ 1*Behavior

messages.body_plain:
I've been using Likert scales that result in data that are fairly normal  - for cfa sem in Lavaan. I've generated plausible model for this data. Now, I also have word freq measures (wf) that are categorical and can't assume they're normally distributed. So I've treated these wfs in separate log linear, logit type analysis. I prefer to have one cfa sem model do the job of both Likert and wf data, and get rid of the separate analysis. In seeking out R functionality online I've been unable to find a documented procedure for it with R, Lavaan. Online sources suggest OpenMX and MPlus. I haven't found a solid reference for R, lavaan, cfa sem categorical and non normal data.

Can I incorporate a categorical variable in cfa sem Lavaan models that can be tested (within the same model) alongside more continuous data like these scale data? I don't want to breach data assumptions.  I believe the categorical data are skewed to the right, with many subjects providing none of the key terms, for example.

I've tried OpenMX but I keep getting 'loading failed' messages (Ubuntu 16.04 LTS) after two attempts and I'm hopeful R Lavaan has the same functionality (in this respect) as OpenMX and MPlus.

Thanks in advance for any pointers.
